title: The Iceberg of Shipping a Real Game
author: Jlannin
selftext:
https://preview.redd.it/zdhfupdke6sh1.png?width=2160&format=png&auto=webp&s=7c9407ffcd581a2e05403a04b0fae8acd8a7eb83

What did I miss? I'd need a lot bigger graphic...  
  
Took me 10 months to get a production quality game out the door (app stores, earning $), starting from scratch; and I would say that my game is essential a clone of others in the HOG genre with some fun twists. This said, it's a worthwhile endeavor - so much to learn to do true agentic development, and games are a great way to learn to build with AI versus traditional methods. Also I didn't have prior game dev experience, like many drawn to this area - although software development was something I know well.  
  
Now I'm confident about how to do more groundbreaking work, like incorporating  live LLM calls into the actual flow of interactions - not just AI as a tool for building more of the same. The models are getting better, but it's a long way from building everything you don't see below the surface with a single goal prompt and a lot of credits.

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body: This is a pretty good list - after first plant I think you’ve got a pretty comprehensive chart here. The only other thing I think you could add is something like “metagame design”. Also, I’ll probably say tuning instead of difficulty, but that’s just semantics.

comments.author: ishmaellius
comments.body:
This is a great post.  Basically describes exactly why most people will never make a real game. 

Demo porn is everywhere these days - and sure - they're a form of fun all of their own, but yea, games they're certainly not.

comments.author: thvaz
comments.body: My first game gathered about 1000 wishlists with $0 money spent on ads. (or on marketing). It wasn't enough, but it was good enough. The learning process was way more vaulable.
